idiom_name: companion-object factory functions (or top-level factory functions) instead of secondary constructors
implementation_notes: Kotlin's coding conventions say to replace overloaded secondary constructors with factory functions, so the named routes live either in the companion object (Money.of(...)) or at top level, where the standard library's listOf/buildList and the List(size) { } fake constructors live; a companion object can even implement an interface, which a JVM static member cannot. The primary constructor is marked private when the factories enforce invariants, and `operator fun invoke` in the companion can make Tree(10) { } read like construction - the conventions consider that less idiomatic than a plainly named factory function, because invocation is not construction.
pitfalls: A companion object is initialized when the class is first resolved, so caches or default instances placed there are created eagerly - use `by lazy` or a top-level object when initialization must be deferred.
`private constructor` closes inheritance as well as direct construction; use internal/protected visibility when subclasses or tests must still create instances.

Java interop reads Kotlin factories as ordinary static methods, so a factory named the same as the class (fake constructor) looks like a constructor to Java callers who cannot see that it may return a subclass.
